findings.text: Iteration fetch releases any previously returned task reference, completes deferred skip work, then yields the next live task with a new reference or null when exhausted.
Iterator teardown unlinks the walk from its current set and drops held references to current set, domain set and current task where present.
Group size query returns the number of tasks currently associated with the given group as observed under serialization.

Live handle acquisition pins the target group, suspends kernfs active protection, takes group mutex and succeeds only for non-dead groups; paired release drops mutex, restores protection and releases the pin.
Offline drain returns holding group mutex only after every live descendant subsystem that is dying has finished going offline.
Attach preparation resolves textual pid input to a referenced task and selects an attach serialization mode; paired finish releases the mode and the reference.
Credential lookup returns a stable reference to the target task credentials that remains valid after return.
Pid cache purge schedules immediate destruction for every cached array of a group and waits until none remain.
Proc reporting emits one row per subsystem with identity, hierarchy, group count and enable state plus a one-time hint when only default hierarchy is visible.
Subsystem enable query reports false when subsystem configuration support is absent, otherwise reflects the per-subsystem enable key state.
When a set offers several task collections, the walk prefers the main collection, then the migrating collection, then the dying collection, and positions at the head of the first non-empty one.
When no further set exists the walk clears its task position so subsequent fetches terminate.
A pinned set remains attached to its group lists across unlock windows, while task departure across steps is compensated by advancing registered iterators whose next task leaves.
When threaded iteration is requested, each outer set establishes its threaded subset walk and current domain reference before being returned; otherwise only outer position advances.
A pending skip is finished before fetching, and entries that are only valid for RCU observation due to zero reference are skipped rather than returned.
Cached pid arrays are distinguished by file kind and by the active pid namespace of the caller observed at lookup or creation time.

Array construction sizes from current membership, collects either thread-group ids or thread ids depending on file kind, ignores non-positive ids, truncates if membership grew, then orders and deduplicates before publishing under the cache entry.
Deduplication assumes ordered input, compacts equal neighbours in place, and reports the count of distinct values, handling empty and singleton inputs without change.
Pid ordering uses ascending numeric comparison of identifier values.

Sequence start revalidates any retained cache handle, reloads when absent, then maps the requested position to the first array element at or after that pid via binary search; next moves linearly and reports termination past the end.

Attach input is stripped and parsed as an integer pid; negative or unparsable input is rejected, zero selects the caller, nonzero selects the named task with not-found reported when absent, and threadgroup mode operates on the group leader.
Tasks flagged non-migratable or marked no-set-affinity are rejected; loss of thread leadership during resolution causes unlock, release and a fresh retry.

Migration permission succeeds for root open credentials or when open effective user matches target real or saved user, otherwise access is denied; release-agent update additionally requires initial user namespace and admin capability.
Notification and clone files expose single flag bits as boolean values with nonzero writes setting and zero writes clearing; sane behavior always reports false.
Group resolution from a kernfs node uses direct private data for directories and parent private data for files, relying on invariant parent linkage.
Set iteration advancement and outer set stepping require the set serialization lock to be already held by the caller.
Task fetch and iterator unlinking acquire the set lock with interrupt state saved and restore it after, keeping the critical section short.
Pid cache lookup, creation, loading, sequence start and stop and delayed destruction are all serialized by the owning group pidlist mutex.
Kn live acquisition orders group mutex outside kernfs active protection by pinning liveness first, breaking protection, then locking; release reverses protection and pin after unlocking.
Release-agent path store and show are serialized by a dedicated spinlock; group size counting uses irq-disabling spin acquisition.
Task resolution and credential acquisition run inside RCU read sections; offline waiting releases group mutex while sleeping and restarts the scan after wakeup.

Pid cache entry holds a key pair of file kind and namespace pointer, a dynamic identifier array with length, list linkage into the owner, an owner back pointer, and delayed work for deferred destruction.
File kind enumeration distinguishes process-group id listing from per-task id listing.

Version one base table defines entries for process listing, clone flag, sane behavior, task listing, notification flag and release agent, binding sequence handlers, numeric handlers or write handlers, root-only restriction where applicable, and a write length bound for the agent path.

Pid cache lifecycle moves from miss to created to loaded to scheduled-for-destruction to destroyed, with reuse cancelling pending destruction and forced purge driving all entries to destroyed before return.

Task walk progresses through outer stepping, optional threaded subset stepping, list selection, per-task fetch, skip completion and terminal state, ending with unlink and release of all held references.
Sequence walk for pid files moves from start lookup through indexed show to linear next steps until past-end null, with stop always arming delayed reclamation and releasing the mutex.
Migration transaction moves from live lock through task resolution and permission gate to attach execution and finally paired finish plus unlock, reporting input length on success.
Offline drain scans live descendants in post order, and upon finding a dying subsystem takes a live reference, waits outside the lock, releases, then restarts until no dying entry remains.

Process and task listing files share sequence handlers parameterized by file kind and share a write path parameterized by threadgroup scope; clone, sane, notification and agent files expose their respective read or show and write handlers.
Proc subsystem statistics file is served by a show handler emitting header plus per-subsystem rows.
Retained cache handle must not be dereferenced after mutex release because asynchronous destruction may have freed it; re-lookup is required.
Membership growth between sizing and collection causes truncation; this race is accepted as indistinguishable from late arrival and must not be treated as an error.
Zero-reference dying entries are unsafe for ordinary iteration and must be skipped even when dead-inclusive iteration is requested.
Delayed destruction must only unlink and free when the work item is no longer pending, otherwise a concurrent reuse would lose the entry.
Dead group handles must be rejected after locking by unlocking and returning null rather than proceeding; offline waiting must not hold group mutex while sleeping.
User-visible file names include process listing, task listing, clone flag, sane behavior, notification flag and release agent, each bound to its handlers in the base table.
Proc statistics output begins with a header naming subsystem, hierarchy, group count and enable columns, followed by one row per subsystem.
Release-agent write length is bounded to one below the maximum path size, and sane behavior output is a fixed false line.
Process listing reports thread-group ids while task listing reports thread ids, selected by the file kind key.
